newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- FEB 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- FEB 21.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek general press:

--Worried government sources said yesterday that the Floisvos affair - the withdrawal of the operating licence for a casino on the Athens seashore, now under investigation by a parliamentary fact-finding commission - is threatening to turn into a politicial crisis centring on former tourism minister Dionyssis Livanos and current Development Minister Vasso Papandreou.
--A draft presidential decree reveals that only a few immigrants will receive the highly-coveted residency card.
--Greeks spent 650 billion drachmas on Lady Luck last year and 230 billion in new casinos alone.
--The war over wages continues: the finance ministry and teachers' union have locked horns over how much newly-appointed high school teachers will actually receive.

--Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos was the victim of burglars recently whose only interest was removing the hard disk in the computer in his office. The ministry says however there were no confidential or compromising documents on the hard disk.

--Members of an alleged guerrilla group for the "liberation" of southern Albania (MAVI) received lenient sentences from an Athens court yesterday for a variety of arms charges. All said they would appeal and have been released.
--As teachers go into their sixth week of strike action, the squabbling over figures with the finance ministry continues.
--There's tension in the air as young conservative opposition New Democracy deputy Costas Karamanlis ponders whether he will accept the invitation to run for leader of the party.
--Members of ruling party PASOK's Central Committee have drafted a list of grievances with the government's policy, and taken a direct shot of Prime Minister Costas Simitis's "court".
--Former Supremer Court President Vassilis Kokkinos is reported to be considering hosting a weekly current affairs show on television.

--Greece will not have summer time this year, as it appears the national economy ministry is in favour of harmonising times with the rest of its European Union partners. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
